To define $ \Delta S_{conf} $ we begin by comparing the adsorption of alkanes in five different zeolite structures: MFI, CHA, TON, FAU, and MOR. Depicted in Figure 2A is the relationship between the entropy of an adsorbed molecule (alkanes and permanent gases) and its gas-phase entropy, where the molecular entropy on the surface never exceeds that in the gas phase. While a significant loss in entropy occurs in all five zeolites, the absolute loss in entropy is distinct for each framework. Adsorbates in TON exhibit the largest loss in entropy upon adsorption, while FAU results in the smallest entropic losses. ABSTRACT: Confinement of hydrocarbons in nanoscale pockets and pores provides tunable capability for controlling molecules in catalysts, sorbents, and membranes for reaction and separation applications. While computation of the enthalpic interactions of hydrocarbons in confined spaces has improved, understanding and predicting the entropy of confined molecules remains a challenge. Here we show, using a set of nine aluminosilicate zeolite frameworks with broad variation in pore and cavity structure, that the entropy of adsorption can be predicted as a linear combination of rotational and translational entropy. The extent of entropy lost upon adsorption is predicted using only a single material descriptor, the occupiable volume ( $ V_{occ} $). Predictive capability of confined molecular entropy permits an understanding of the relation with adsorption enthalpy, the ability to computationally screen microporous materials, and an understanding of the role of confinement on the kinetics of molecules in confined spaces.

On the basis of this shape-selective feature , highly effective molecular separations and selective catalytic conversions can be achieved within zeolitic structures that are difficult to accomplish with other materials and/or techniques . $ ^ { 1-3 } $ So far, several shape-selectivity mechanisms have been elucidated and applications identified. $ ^{2-18} $ In common molecular sieving, bulky molecules adsorb preferentially over bulkier species as a result of steric constraints imposed by the zeolites' framework, e.g., linear alkane molecules compared to branched isomers. $ ^{19-23} $ Besides this common adsorption competition based on molecular bulkiness, the reverse phenomenon can also occur, i.e., competitive adsorption in favor of the bulkier species. Experiments revealed preferential adsorption of branched alkanes over their linear isomers on specific zeolites with tubular pore systems such as SAPO-5 and Mordenite. $ ^{24-28} $ Molecular simulations indicated that in such zeolites, depending on conditions, branched alkanes are preferentially adsorbed at the expense of linear isomers. $ ^{29-34} $ The present manuscript discusses the mechanisms of shape selectivity in n- and isoalkane adsorption on zeolite MCM-22. This zeolite with IZA code MWW is a relatively new synthetic material that has an unusual and quite complex pore structure. $ ^{35} $ Its framework is composed of two independent pore systems. The enthalpy and the entropy contributions to the Gibbs free energies were calculated at T = 298 K and partial pressure of 1 atm (101325 Pa). The enthalpy (H) of gas-phase pyridine and acetonitrile molecules is defined as the sum of total electronic energy ( $ E_{el} $), internal vibrational energy ( $ E_{v} $), zero-point vibrational energy (ZPVE), as well as the rotational and translational contributions to the internal energy: $ H = E_{el} + E_{v} + ZPVE + E_{R} + E_{t} $. The corresponding calculated entropies (S) includes translational, ( $ S_{t} $) vibrational, ( $ S_{v} $) and rotational ( $ S_{r} $) degrees of freedom: $ S = S_{t} + S_{v} + S_{r} $. All the considered systems are in singlet state, thus the electronic contribution to the entropy is zero. Since both adsorbed molecules are constrained in the zeolite cavity their entropy contributions in the adsorption complexes were corrected as follows: the translational and rotational degrees of freedom were reduced by 1 and 1.28 [37]. The Gibbs free energies of the zeolite support consist of only vibrational and electronic contributions. The expressions of all enthalpy and entropy contributions can be found in Ref. [38].

The first attempts to describe guest-induced flexibility in zeolites were done using molecular dynamics simulations. $ ^{79-82} $ Rigid zeolitic force fields were dynamically modified using transition state theory to include lattice flexibility, and the results obtained by these models were in good agreement with experimental data. $ ^{79-81,83,84} $ It was shown that framework flexibility in silicalite-1 (MFI-type framework) is responsible for the adsorption of large molecules such as isobutane and heptane with inflection behavior at high loadings, $ ^{80} $ while enhanced self-diffusivity at low loadings of short alkanes (i.e. methane and n-butane) was observed. $ ^{81} $ Framework flexibility is also crucial for aromatics adsorption on MFI zeolite, especially at high pressures. $ ^{84,85} $ While the use of rigid zeolitic models led to the underestimation of the aromatics adsorption in MFI zeolite by a factor of two, $ ^{84,85} $ the use of flexible models to simulate diffusion coefficients of various alkanes in silicalite-1 zeolite resulted in a convergence of experimental and theoretical values. $ ^{86} $ Recently by using in situ integrated differential phase contrast scanning transmission electron microscopy (iDPC-STEM) while adsorbing benzene molecules on MFI zeolite, Xiong et al. showed that the MFI structure goes through severe deformations giving another proof of guest-induced flexibility in zeolites (see Fig. 4). $ ^{87} $

2.4.4. Trapdoor. Traditional diﬀusion models primarily consider two types of interactions: those between guest molecules (guest–guest) and those between guest molecules and the zeolite framework (guest–host). However, when cations are present in the zeolite structure, a third interaction—involving guest molecules, the framework, and cations (guest–host-cation)—must also be accounted for. A striking example of such ternary interactions is the well-known ‘‘molecular trapdoor’’. This phenomenon, also referred to as the ‘‘gating effect’’, describes a unique molecular sieving mechanism in certain zeolites and related porous materi- als. In the following appendix , we derive the entropy of adsorption in the case of infinite dilution and show how it may be related to familiar thermodynamic quantities ( cf . eq 5 ) . To begin , we define our adsorption entropy in the limit of infinite dilution via

$$ \Delta s_{\mathrm{ads}}^{\infty}=\lim_{N/V\rightarrow0}\left[\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{V,T,\mathrm{ads}}-\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{V,T,\mathrm{gas}}\right] $$

$$ =S_{ads}(N=1,V,T)-S_{gas}(N=1,V,T) $$

where the subscripts “ads” and “gas” labels identify the adsorbed (confined) and gas (bulk) phases, respectively. Given the constraints of a fixed number of molecules (N), volume (V), and temperature (T), it is natural to continue working in the canonical ensemble. (As in the main text, lowercase symbols identify intensive molecular or molar properties, whereas the uppercase indicates an extensive property.) For the molecules that we examine in this work (e.g., rigid molecules with no internal degrees of freedom), the canonical partition function Q may be expressed as

$$ \begin{aligned}Q(N,V,T)&=Q_{trans}(N,V,T)Q_{rot}(N,V,T)\\&\quad\times Z(N,V,T)\end{aligned} $$

where $ Q_{trans} $ and $ Q_{rot} $ are the translational and rotational partition functions (which are unaffected by confinement) and Z is the configurational partition function. The translational and rotational partition functions are available in the usual statistical mechanics texts $ ^{44,45} $ but are ultimately unimportant for the derivation that follows.

descriptor_candidates.name: occ_vol_confinement_entropy_ratio
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: The adsorption entropy loss (in units of R) for pure-silica zeolite/adsorbate systems increases with the log of the ratio of the gravimetric accessible volume AV (cm^3/g, intrinsic pore measure) to the volumetric occupiable volume estimate Vol/density (per-mass pore volume from molecular descriptor and source-scale density); a formula using only this log-ratio will achieve lower MAE of entropy loss/R than the full 14-input network baseline is NOT claimed, but this single re-expressed feature will capture the dominant confinement contribution, with the hypothesis falsified if adding the remaining 10 molecular-shape inputs does not improve MAE by more than a pre-specified threshold (e.g., 0.05 R).
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence (E02) reports that adsorbed entropy loss across nine zeolite frameworks is predicted by the single descriptor occupiable volume V_occ; E01 shows entropy loss varies by framework (TON largest, FAU smallest). Mechanism (inference): tighter confinement reduces translational/rotational freedom of the adsorbate; the AV-to-pore-volume ratio distinguishes accessible channel volume from total cage volume, discriminating channel-like (large entropy loss) from cage-like (small loss) frameworks even at equal total pore volume.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Fit a regression of entropy loss/R on log(AV/(Vol/density)); compute MAE. If the residual MAE is not statistically reduced versus a volume-only model, or if the fitted sign of the coefficient contradicts the confinement mechanism (larger ratio -> larger loss), the hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: shape_anisotropy_rotational_loss
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Adsorbate rotational entropy loss upon confinement scales with the degree of molecular shape anisotropy as captured by the log-ratio of the extreme principal moments of inertia PMI1 and PMI3 relative to the intermediate moment PMI2; molecules with higher anisotropy (rod-like or plate-like, e.g., linear alkanes) lose a larger fraction of their rotational entropy in channels than near-spherical molecules, so this descriptor alone will correlate with entropy loss/R with a positive monotonic relationship, falsified if the correlation sign is negative or |Spearman rho| < 0.2 on held-out data.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence (E01) decomposes entropy loss into translational and rotational components for linear alkanes and shows rotational entropy fraction of gas-phase entropy differs by molecule; E05 notes rotational degrees of freedom are reduced by a fixed factor in confined complexes. Mechanism (inference): rotational freedom loss depends on how anisotropic the molecule is relative to pore geometry; a near-spherical molecule retains more rotational entropy in any pore, while an anisotropic molecule is orientationally constrained in one-dimensional channels.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Compute Spearman correlation of entropy loss/R with log((PMI1*PMI3)/(PMI2^2+1)) across the dataset. Falsify if the correlation is not positive and significant (p > 0.05), or if including this descriptor alongside AV in the nonlinear network yields no MAE improvement over AV alone.

descriptor_candidates.name: aperture_mismatch_freedom_index
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss is governed by the mismatch between framework limiting pore size (lsd_f) and probe-accessible pore size (lsd_p), modulated by molecular smallest dimension PBF; when |lsd_f - lsd_p| is large relative to the molecular cross-section PBF, the adsorbate sits in a loose, cavity-like environment with small entropy loss, whereas near-zero mismatch forces tight packing with large entropy loss. This descriptor will reduce MAE of entropy loss/R relative to a model using AV alone, falsified if the MAE does not improve or if the fitted relationship is not the predicted non-monotonic (minimum near mismatch ~ PBF) form.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence (E04) shows shape selectivity and distinct adsorption states arise from close matching between molecular dimensions and pore windows; E10 notes molecules can distort to fit pores up to ~20% smaller than their free size, implying a window-size tolerance regime; E06 describes framework flexibility enabling adsorption of larger guests. Mechanism (inference): entropy loss depends on the ratio of free volume around the adsorbate to molecular volume, which is controlled jointly by framework pore size, accessible (probe) pore size, and molecular smallest cross-section; the squared mismatch term with log damping expresses the predicted loose-fit vs tight-fit regime without assuming units for the density field.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Train the nonlinear network on all 14 inputs and separately on a reduced set replacing raw lsd_f, lsd_p, PBF with this single derived descriptor; compare MAE of entropy loss/R via cross-validation. Falsify if (i) the descriptor model's MAE is worse than AV-only, or (ii) the empirical relationship between descriptor and entropy loss is monotonic over the full range, contradicting the predicted tight-fit penalty peaking near zero mismatch.

descriptor_candidates.name: channel_cage_dimensionless_pore_ratio
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss/R scales positively with a dimensionless combination of the framework limiting dimension lsd_f and the ratio of gravimetric accessible volume AV to per-mass pore volume Vol/density: frameworks whose accessible volume is a large fraction of total pore volume (channel-like) force tighter packing at fixed limiting dimension and thus larger entropy loss, whereas cage-like frameworks (small ratio) show smaller loss. This single descriptor will achieve lower MAE of entropy loss/R than the retained aperture_mismatch_freedom_index (0.5416), falsified if MAE is not improved or if the fitted monotonic trend is negative.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence: E02 reports occupiable volume as a single material descriptor predicting entropy loss; E01 shows framework-dependent loss (TON largest, FAU smallest), i.e., channel vs cage topology matters beyond total volume. Inference (mechanism): the AV/(Vol/density) ratio separates connected channel volume from total cavity volume; multiplying by lsd_f^2 introduces the length-scale of the confining walls, so the descriptor grows for long tight channels and saturates via the log for large cavities, matching the channel-vs-cage discrimination mechanism.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Train the nonlinear network with all 14 native inputs replaced (in part) by this descriptor; compare cross-validated MAE of entropy loss/R against the retained round-2 descriptor. Falsify if MAE >= 0.5416 or if the empirical descriptor-entropy relationship is not positive and monotonic.

descriptor_candidates.name: asphericity_pore_span_loss_index
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss/R increases with the product of molecular elongation measures (SPAN, GeDi) relative to the smallest molecular dimension PBF, damped by the ratio of total accessible surface area ASA to the molecular LabuteASA: elongated molecules in frameworks whose gravimetric surface area per unit molecular surface is small (tight wall contact) lose more rotational/translational entropy. The descriptor will reduce MAE below the round-2 baseline, falsified if the fitted relationship is non-positive or MAE does not improve.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence: E01 decomposes entropy loss into translational and rotational components for linear alkanes, showing shape-dependent losses; E09 derives adsorption entropy from the configurational partition function, which for rigid molecules depends on accessible configurational space set by molecular shape vs pore walls. Inference (mechanism): SPAN*GeDi/PBF is a dimensionless asphericity factor measuring how much a molecule must orient to fit; ASA/LabuteASA contrasts framework surface availability per mass with molecular surface, so large asphericity with limited surface freedom implies orientational pinning and larger entropy loss.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Cross-validated MAE comparison against the retained descriptor; additionally test Spearman correlation of the descriptor with entropy loss/R. Falsify if rho is not positive with p < 0.05, or if MAE fails to improve over 0.5416.

descriptor_candidates.name: inertia_weighted_pore_confinement
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss/R scales with the total molecular rotational inertia (sum of principal moments PMI1+PMI2+PMI3) divided by the product of accessible volume and the square of the framework limiting dimension: heavy, high-inertia molecules in small, low-accessible-volume frameworks lose more entropy because confinement converts more of their rotational and translational freedom into hindered motion, and the effect strengthens as the confining length scale lsd_f shrinks. The descriptor will lower MAE of entropy loss/R relative to the round-2 retained descriptor, falsified if the fitted coefficient sign is negative or MAE does not improve.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence: E05 shows adsorbed molecules in zeolite cavities require reduction factors on translational and rotational degrees of freedom (1 and 1.28), i.e., both modes are suppressed upon confinement; E01 shows gas-phase entropy and its loss vary systematically with molecular identity. Inference (mechanism): rotational entropy of a molecule scales with its principal moments of inertia; dividing by AV*lsd_f^2 (a volume times a length-squared, giving a confinement-density-like term weighted by source-scale density) expresses the confinement strength per unit of molecular rotational inertia, unifying molecular and framework contributions in one dimensionless-like quantity.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Fit the nonlinear network with this descriptor among inputs and compare cross-validated MAE of entropy loss/R to 0.5416; additionally check the partial dependence direction. Falsify if MAE fails to improve, or if the descriptor-entropy relationship is decreasing rather than increasing over the observed range.

candidates.falsification_criteria: Cross-validated MAE comparison against the retained descriptor; additionally test Spearman correlation of the descriptor with entropy loss/R. Falsify if rho is not positive with p < 0.05, or if MAE fails to improve over 0.5416.

candidates.name: inertia_weighted_pore_confinement
candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss/R scales with the total molecular rotational inertia (sum of principal moments PMI1+PMI2+PMI3) divided by the product of accessible volume and the square of the framework limiting dimension: heavy, high-inertia molecules in small, low-accessible-volume frameworks lose more entropy because confinement converts more of their rotational and translational freedom into hindered motion, and the effect strengthens as the confining length scale lsd_f shrinks. The descriptor will lower MAE of entropy loss/R relative to the round-2 retained descriptor, falsified if the fitted coefficient sign is negative or MAE does not improve.
candidates.rationale: Source evidence: E05 shows adsorbed molecules in zeolite cavities require reduction factors on translational and rotational degrees of freedom (1 and 1.28), i.e., both modes are suppressed upon confinement; E01 shows gas-phase entropy and its loss vary systematically with molecular identity. Inference (mechanism): rotational entropy of a molecule scales with its principal moments of inertia; dividing by AV*lsd_f^2 (a volume times a length-squared, giving a confinement-density-like term weighted by source-scale density) expresses the confinement strength per unit of molecular rotational inertia, unifying molecular and framework contributions in one dimensionless-like quantity.
candidates.falsification_criteria: Fit the nonlinear network with this descriptor among inputs and compare cross-validated MAE of entropy loss/R to 0.5416; additionally check the partial dependence direction. Falsify if MAE fails to improve, or if the descriptor-entropy relationship is decreasing rather than increasing over the observed range.

descriptor_candidates.name: free_volume_per_contact_area_index
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss/R decreases with the free-volume-per-molecular-surface ratio: frameworks offering more accessible volume per unit of molecular contact surface allow the adsorbate to retain more positional freedom, while low AV relative to molecular surface area forces wall contact and larger entropy loss. This descriptor will improve MAE of entropy loss/R below 0.5416 relative to the retained aperture_mismatch_freedom_index.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence (E02) identifies occupiable volume as the dominant single material descriptor; E09 shows entropy loss is governed by the configurational partition function, i.e., the accessible configurational space. Inference (mechanism): configurational freedom scales with free volume but is penalized by the molecular surface area in contact with pore walls; dividing the volumetric pore quantity (AV * density on the source scale, a per-molecule-like pore volume) by LabuteASA yields a free-volume-per-wall-contact measure that distinguishes tight-contact channels (TON-like, large loss) from spacious cages (FAU-like, small loss).
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Fit the network with all 14 native inputs and this descriptor replacing raw AV and LabuteASA; compare cross-validated MAE of entropy loss/R to 0.5416. Falsify if MAE does not improve, or if the empirical descriptor-entropy relationship is not negative and monotonic.

descriptor_candidates.name: inertia_contrast_confinement_ratio
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss/R increases with the contrast between the intermediate principal moment PMI2 and the geometric mean of the extreme moments, multiplied by the ratio of framework limiting dimension to molecular smallest dimension: molecules whose rotational inertia is concentrated in one axis (disc-like or anisotropic rotors) confined in pores whose limiting dimension exceeds their smallest cross-section lose more rotational entropy because the accessible orientation space shrinks non-uniformly. This descriptor will achieve MAE below 0.5416.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence (E01) shows rotational entropy loss depends on molecular shape, and (E07) shows molecular symmetry strongly alters rotational dynamics under confinement. Inference (mechanism): the PMI contrast term quantifies how asymmetric the rotational phase space is, while lsd_f/PBF expresses the geometric clearance of the pore; large clearance for an asymmetric rotor means only a narrow set of orientations fit the channel axis, so the rotational partition function collapses disproportionately. Both factors together predict a positive synergistic effect absent from either term alone.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Train with all 14 inputs, replacing PMI1, PMI2, PMI3, lsd_f, PBF by this descriptor; compare cross-validated MAE of entropy loss/R against 0.5416. Falsify if MAE does not improve, or if the product form shows no positive interaction (partial dependence of the PMI-contrast term is flat at both high and low lsd_f/PBF).

descriptor_candidates.name: span_normalized_tortuosity_index
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss/R increases with the sum of two additive terms: (i) molecular elongation asymmetry |SPAN - GeDi| normalized by the molecular characteristic length Vol^(1/3), which measures the orientational cost of threading through narrow windows, and (ii) the probe-to-framework pore ratio lsd_p/lsd_f, which measures how much of the nominal framework pore is truly accessible. Linear (additive) combination of these two independent mechanisms — molecular threading cost and framework accessibility — will reduce MAE below 0.5416; the additive (rather than multiplicative) structure is itself falsifiable.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence (E04) shows close size matching between molecule and pore window creates distinct adsorption states; E10 shows molecules distort up to ~20% to enter smaller pores, implying a threading penalty. Inference (mechanism): |SPAN - GeDi| captures the gap between the longest and geometric dimension, distinguishing compact from rod-like threading requirements independent of PBF (which already appears in the retained descriptor), while lsd_p/lsd_f quantifies whether windows or cavities dominate accessibility. Their additivity reflects the hypothesis that translational (threading) and orientational (window-matching) entropy losses are independent contributions.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Train the network with SPAN, GeDi, Vol, lsd_p, lsd_f replaced by this descriptor and compare cross-validated MAE of entropy loss/R to 0.5416. Falsify if MAE does not improve, or if a multiplicative variant of the two terms significantly outperforms the additive one, contradicting the independence-of-mechanisms claim.

retained.name: aperture_mismatch_freedom_index
retained.hypothesis: Entropy loss is governed by the mismatch between framework limiting pore size (lsd_f) and probe-accessible pore size (lsd_p), modulated by molecular smallest dimension PBF; when |lsd_f - lsd_p| is large relative to the molecular cross-section PBF, the adsorbate sits in a loose, cavity-like environment with small entropy loss, whereas near-zero mismatch forces tight packing with large entropy loss. This descriptor will reduce MAE of entropy loss/R relative to a model using AV alone, falsified if the MAE does not improve or if the fitted relationship is not the predicted non-monotonic (minimum near mismatch ~ PBF) form.
